summary: Hungary lies in the Carpathian Basin in Central Europe, was founded by the Magyars who migrated in during the 9th century, and is known for its thermal springs, for Budapest on the Danube, and for Hungarian paprika.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Around the year 1000 the Hungarian grand prince Stephen I accepted a crown from the Pope and was crowned, enforcing Catholicism and ending the pagan age of the Magyars, and he was later venerated as a saint. The Reformation of the 16th century at one point led most of the country to convert to Protestantism, but in the 17th century the Habsburgs launched the Counter-Reformation, promoted by Cardinal Péter Pázmány and others, which re-Catholicized the west and north. From 1949 to 1989 the communist regime suppressed the church, and Cardinal József Mindszenty was imprisoned; together with recent secularization, the proportion of believers has continued to fall, and in the 2022 census a large number of people did not answer the question on religion.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: From 1949 to 1989 the communist regime promoted atheist education and restricted religious activity, so that many families no longer passed on their faith, and urbanization and modernization accelerated secularization. In the 2022 census about forty percent of people chose not to answer the religion question, so the number of non-believers may in reality be higher than the statistics show.

ranking.name: Reformed Church (Calvinism)
ranking.description: During the Reformation of the 16th century Calvinism spread rapidly in eastern Hungary, and Debrecen therefore became known as the "Calvinist Rome". At that time most of the country was under Ottoman rule, so the Habsburgs could not carry out the Counter-Reformation; the Edict of Torda of 1568 in Transylvania was one of the earliest religious toleration laws in Europe. The Reformed Church has therefore been deeply rooted in the Great Plain in the east and has been regarded as the "Hungarian religion".

ranking.name: Lutheranism
ranking.description: Lutheranism was accepted in the 16th century mainly by German-speaking townspeople and Slovaks, and is found in the west and north. After the Counter-Reformation of the 17th century the number of followers fell, but it has continued to this day, with some German and Slovak communities preserving the Lutheran tradition.

ranking.name: Greek Catholic Church
ranking.description: Greek Catholics use the Byzantine rite but recognize the Roman Pope. They are mainly descendants of the Rusyns and Romanians of the north-east; the Union of Uzhhorod of 1646 brought the original Orthodox believers into the Catholic Church, and in 1912 the Eparchy of Hajdúdorog was established, where services are held in Hungarian.

religion.background: Hungary became a Catholic kingdom under Stephen I in 1000; after the Reformation of the 16th century large numbers of people converted to Calvinism and Lutheranism, while in the same period the Ottoman Empire occupied the center for a hundred and fifty years, splitting Hungary into three parts. The Habsburg Counter-Reformation of the 17th century made Catholicism the majority again, while Protestantism kept its strength in the east. In World War II in the 20th century more than half a million Hungarian Jews were killed, and after 1949 the communist regime suppressed religion. After democratization in 1989 religious freedom was restored, but society had become quite secular.

ranking.name: Hungarian
ranking.description: Hungarian belongs to the Ugric branch of the Uralic family and is entirely different from the surrounding Slavic and Germanic languages. The Magyars migrated into the Carpathian Basin from the east around 895–896, bringing this language. The Funeral Sermon and Prayer of the late 12th century is the earliest surviving continuous Hungarian text. From the Middle Ages to the 19th century Latin was long the official language; the "language reform movement" of the late 18th to early 19th century created a large number of new words, and Hungarian became the official language only in 1844. The Treaty of Trianon of 1920 made about three million Hungarian speakers minorities in neighboring countries.

ranking.name: German
ranking.description: After the Ottomans were driven out in the 18th century, the Habsburgs recruited large numbers of German settlers to cultivate the devastated land, forming the "Danube Swabian" communities. In 1946–1948 after World War II, about two hundred thousand ethnic Germans were expelled to Germany, and the German-speaking minority that remained still has German schools and cultural organizations today.

ranking.name: Romani
ranking.description: The Roma arrived in Hungary around the 15th century; some speak Romani, some speak Beás, a language derived from Old Romanian, but most now have Hungarian as their mother tongue. The Minorities Act of 1993 recognized the Roma as a minority and guaranteed their language rights, but Roma communities still face discrimination in education and employment.

language.history: The ancestors of Hungarian came from the Ural Mountains region, and after the Magyars settled in the Carpathian Basin at the end of the 9th century they absorbed a large number of Slavic, Turkic and German loanwords. The medieval Kingdom of Hungary used Latin as its official and scholarly language, and Hungarian was used mainly in speech and religious literature. The language reform movement and nationalism of the 18th–19th centuries brought Hungarian official status in 1844. After the Treaty of Trianon of 1920, Hungary itself became an almost single-language society, while large numbers of Hungarian speakers remained in neighboring countries such as Romania, Slovakia and Serbia.

ranking.name: Goulash (gulyás)
ranking.description: A thick soup boiled from beef, onion, potato, carrot, caraway and plenty of paprika, with a bright red color and a slightly spicy, rich flavor.
ranking.history: The "gulyás" in the name originally meant the herdsmen who pastured cattle on the Great Hungarian Plain, and the soup was first food that herdsmen stewed outdoors in a large iron cauldron. Paprika is native to the Americas and was introduced to Hungary via the Ottoman Empire in the 16th–17th centuries, and became the core spice of Hungarian cuisine only after the 18th century. When Hungarian nationalism rose in the 19th century, people took this humble soup as a national symbol against Habsburg German culture, and it has been Hungary's national dish ever since.

ranking.name: Lángos
ranking.description: Fermented dough is pressed into a large round, deep-fried, rubbed while hot with garlic oil, and topped with sour cream and grated cheese, crisp outside, soft inside and very fragrant.
ranking.history: The name comes from the Hungarian "láng" (flame); it was originally the flat bread that farm families baked in front of the oven flames when baking bread. It later evolved into a fried version, which in the 20th century became the most popular street snack at markets, swimming pools and the shores of Lake Balaton. In the communist period it was a cheap and filling national snack, and today it is still a must-eat for Hungarians on summer holidays.

ranking.name: Chicken paprikash (csirkepaprikás)
ranking.description: Chicken is stewed with onion and paprika, and at the end sour cream is added to turn the sauce into a thick orange-red sauce, served with Hungarian small dumplings (nokedli).
ranking.history: Chicken paprikash is one of the most representative dishes since the spread of Hungarian paprika cooking in the 19th century, common in homes and a classic dish in Budapest restaurants. In the novel Dracula, published in 1897, the protagonist eats a dish of "paprika hendl" on his way to Transylvania, showing that it was already a Hungarian dish familiar to foreign travelers at that time. It remains a classic of Hungarian family Sunday lunches.

ranking.name: Dobos torte
ranking.description: Six thin sponge layers are sandwiched with chocolate buttercream, and the top is covered with a hard slice of caramel, so that neat layers can be seen when it is cut.
ranking.history: The Dobos torte was invented by the Budapest confectioner József Dobos and was exhibited at the Hungarian National Exhibition of 1885, where even Emperor Franz Joseph of Austria-Hungary and Empress Elisabeth tasted it. The caramel slice on top prevents the cake from drying out, allowing it to keep longer and be shipped to various places in an age without refrigeration. Dobos published the recipe only in 1906, and it has since become the representative dessert of Hungarian café culture.

ranking.name: Fisherman's soup (halászlé)
ranking.description: A spicy red fish soup boiled from freshwater fish such as carp and catfish with plenty of paprika and onion, bright red with a rich aroma, eaten with bread.
ranking.history: Hungary has no coastline, so the freshwater fish of the Danube and Tisza have been an important food since ancient times, and halászlé was originally a dish that fishermen stewed in a big iron cauldron by the river. Szeged and Baja each have different methods and often compare whose is more authentic, and a halászlé festival is held every year. Because of the Catholic tradition of not eating meat on Christmas Eve, halászlé has become the main course of Christmas Eve dinner in many Hungarian families.
